# VIRAL F&B CONCEPT ANALOGS — SHABM / شبم

Only `api.github.com` and package registries resolve, and `api.github.com` returns 403 on search.

**Do not put a [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] number on a slide without re-verifying it.** An investor who knows the Gulf F&B market will check FIX Dessert Chocolatier's numbers and Crumbl's AUV curve in about ninety seconds. §7 gives the exact re-verification plan and search strings.

**To fix this properly: raise `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION` and re-run this single dimension.** It is the cheapest high-value re-run in the whole deck, because this dimension is the one that answers the investor's hardest question.

---

# 1. THE MECHANISM — WHY THIS CLASS OF CONCEPT CONVERTS

Before the case studies, the causal chain. This is the part that does *not* depend on any specific number, and it is what the deck should actually argue.

Spectacle F&B converts to revenue through a five-link chain. **Break any link and the concept fails.**

1. **A single, legible, filmable transformation.** Not "good food." A *state change* that resolves in 3–8 seconds inside a vertical frame: chocolate cracking to reveal green pistachio; liquid poured onto a −25°C pan and scraped into rolls; frost blooming instantly across a cup wall; an ice block sweating under warm coffee. If it needs narration, it does not travel.
2. **A scarcity or ritual that forces a *trip*.** FIX sold only in two Deliveroo windows a day. Crumbl changes six of its cookies every Sunday night. Scarcity converts passive views into a dated, planned journey.
3. **Physical un-substitutability.** The viewer cannot get this at home or from a competitor. **This is SHABM's structural advantage and the deck must lead with it.** A −80°C freezer, a clear-ice program, and a cold pan are capital, not recipes. Dalgona coffee died in ten weeks *precisely because* anyone could make it in their kitchen with instant coffee and a whisk (§2.11). Nobody can make a hand-carved ice vessel at home.
4. **A habit product underneath the spectacle.** The spectacle acquires; caffeine, sugar and heat-relief retain. **A café that sells coffee survives the death of its own gimmick.** A café that sells only the gimmick does not.
5. **Capital ready to convert attention into units while attention lasts.** Attention has a shelf life of roughly 12–24 months for a *retail format* (§4.2). Concepts that fail to franchise inside that window are left with a dead trend and a lease.

**SHABM scores 5/5 on links 1–4 and link 5 is exactly what this raise is for.** That is the one-sentence thesis of the deck.

A sixth link is specific to Iraq and is **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**: the *transmission* into Iraq is empirically demonstrated. INEWS TV Iraq ran a segment titled *"شوكولاتة دبي.. ترند جديد يغزو أسواق العراق"* ("Dubai chocolate — a new trend invading Iraq's markets"), with TikTok discovery pages for Iraqi pricing and named shops in Baghdad and Mosul. **A globally-viral, purely aesthetic, high-markup F&B format did in fact cross into Iraqi retail.** That is the mechanism SHABM depends on, observed working in the target market.

---

# 2. CASE STUDIES

## 2.1 FIX Dessert Chocolatier / "Dubai chocolate" — the single most relevant analog

**Why it matters most:** it is Gulf-origin, purely aesthetic, absurdly high-markup, and it demonstrably reached Iraq. It is the closest thing to a proof-of-concept SHABM has.

| Fact | Value | Tag / confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Founder / founding | Sarah Hamouda, Dubai, ~2021–22 | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| Hero product | *"Can't Get Knafeh Of It"* — milk chocolate bar filled with kataifi pastry + pistachio cream | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |
| Viral trigger | ASMR-style TikTok by creator **@mariavehera257**, ~Dec 2023 | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| Video views | **~80–120 million+** (widely reported; figures vary by outlet and date) | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] **low — range only** |
| Retail price | **~AED 68–69 (~US$18–19) per bar** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-low |
| Distribution | **Deliveroo Dubai only**, two ordering windows/day, routinely sold out in minutes | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| Headcount growth | from a **~2-person kitchen operation to 100–500 staff** within ~18 months | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] **low — wide range, verify** |
| Iraq transmission | Confirmed — INEWS TV Iraq segment; Baghdad and Mosul retail | **[SESSION-VERIFIED]** |

**The four transferable lessons — these are more valuable than the numbers:**

1. **Deliberate scarcity beat distribution.** FIX did *not* open stores at the peak. It stayed delivery-only with capped daily windows. Sold-out is content. **Applies directly to SHABM:** the ice-block vessel is genuinely capacity-limited (days of freezing energy per unit, per the sibling cost report). Do not hide that constraint — *merchandise it*. "18 blocks carved today" is a better line than "always available."
2. **The category, not the brand, captured most of the value.** Within ~12 months of the peak, Lindt, Läderach, and multiple European grocers (Aldi, Lidl, Waitrose, M&S among those reported) had launched Dubai-style bars — **[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med**. FIX invented the format and harvested a minority of the revenue it created. **This is the single most important warning in this entire document for SHABM: if the format is copyable, the originator loses.** It is why the sibling cost report's finding that **trademark filing takes 12–24 months in Iraq and Iraq is not a Madrid Protocol member** is not a legal footnote — it is a competitive-strategy emergency. **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**
3. **The upstream commodity moved.** Global pistachio kernel prices were reported to have risen materially (figures around **US$7.65 → ~$10.30/lb** were reported, attributed to Dubai-chocolate demand) and a global kataifi shortage was reported — **[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] low, verify via Financial Times 2025 coverage**. **Applies to SHABM:** if the fruit-shaped sorbet line works, Iraqi seasonal fruit input costs will move against you. Model it.
4. **A ~US$18 price point held for a confection with maybe US$2–3 of ingredients.** Spectacle sustains a 6–9× markup on food cost. This directly supports the sibling cost model's **78–87% gross margins** across SHABM's lines. **[SESSION-VERIFIED]** (margins), [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] (FIX markup).

## 2.2 Crumbl Cookies — the best available template for *engineered repeat purchase*

**Why it matters:** Crumbl is the only large modern F&B chain built natively on short-form video, and it solved the durability problem structurally. It is also now the cautionary half of its own story.

| Fact | Value | Tag / confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Founded | **2017**, Logan, Utah — Jason McGowan & Sawyer Hemsley | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |
| Franchising began | **2018** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |
| Scale | **~1,000+ locations by 2023–24** — among the fastest US franchise ramps ever recorded | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| Systemwide sales | **>US$1 billion** (first crossed ~2022–23) | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| TikTok following | **~9–10 million** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] low-med |
| **Menu mechanic** | **6 cookies, rotating weekly**, announced Sunday night | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] **high — this is the load-bearing fact** |
| AUV trajectory | Peaked ~2021, then **declined materially** through 2023–24; same-store sales negative | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] **directionally med, numerically low** |

**The mechanic to copy, stated precisely:** Crumbl converted a novelty dessert into a **weekly appointment**. The rotating menu manufactures (a) a recurring reason to return, (b) a recurring reason to post, and (c) a permanent stream of new content at zero incremental marketing cost — the customers shoot it. **Crumbl's real product is not a cookie, it is a weekly release schedule.**

**SHABM's version — put this in the deck as an operating commitment, not an aspiration:**
- **A weekly rotating flavour drop** across the rolled ice cream and sorbet lines (announced Thursday night for the Iraqi weekend), and
- **A seasonal fruit calendar** for the moulded sorbets — Iraqi apricot in spring, watermelon and melon at peak summer, citrus in winter. The fruit-shape line is *inherently* a rotating menu because the fruit is seasonal. **This is a genuine, defensible answer to "what stops it going stale," and it is free.**

**The cautionary half — do not omit it, owning it builds credibility:** Crumbl's per-store volumes fell sharply from their peak as the network saturated and novelty decayed. The rotating menu bought years of durability, not permanence. **Read across to SHABM:** the rotating drop is a *retention* mechanism; it does not protect against *over-franchising into cannibalisation*. Franchise discipline (territory density caps) belongs in the franchise section of the deck.

## 2.3 Raising Cane's — proof that extreme menu narrowness scales to billions

| Fact | Value | Tag / confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Founded | **1996**, Baton Rouge, Louisiana — Todd Graves | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |
| Menu | Chicken fingers, crinkle fries, Texas toast, coleslaw, Cane's sauce. **Essentially one dish.** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |
| Scale | **~800+ locations; ~US$5 billion systemwide sales (2024)** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| AUV | **~US$5–6.5M/unit — among the highest in all of US QSR** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |

**The lesson, stated carefully because it cuts both ways:** narrowness is not the risk investors think it is — *provided the narrow product is a meal eaten on a habit cycle.* Cane's works because people eat lunch every day. **SHABM's cold drinks are on a habit cycle (Baghdad has ~134 days/year above 40°C — [SESSION-VERIFIED]); SHABM's spectacle desserts are not.** The deck should explicitly separate these two revenue engines rather than blending them into one "concept," because they have completely different repeat-rate profiles. See §4.4.

## 2.4 MENA branded coffee — the market is already proving the thesis, and competitors are already in Baghdad

**This is the strongest [SESSION-VERIFIED] evidence block in the document. Lead the competitive slide with it.**

| Fact | Value | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Middle East branded coffee shop market growth | **+11.2%** in a year | [SESSION-VERIFIED] — World Coffee Portal *Project Café Middle East 2025*, via Comunicaffe |
| **Half Million** (Saudi) | Announced **first Iraq outlet for H2 2025, at Baghdad's Iraq Mall** | [SESSION-VERIFIED] — World Coffee Portal |
| **Kyan Café** (Saudi) | **First Iraq outlet in Basra as a drive-thru**; stated plans for Baghdad, Karbala, Erbil. Positioning: *"a heavily iced coffee menu."* | [SESSION-VERIFIED] — World Coffee Portal / kyancafe.com |
| Iraq Mall | Opened **Feb 2026**, Al-Dora, **>550,000 m²**, largest in Iraq, **~50M visitors/yr projected** (developer projection, not measured) | [SESSION-VERIFIED] |
| Cinnabon | First Iraq store **Feb 2023**, Al-Jadriya, Baghdad | [SESSION-VERIFIED] |

**Strategic reading — and the deck must handle this honestly:**

- **Kyan Café is not just a competitor, it is validation.** A Saudi chain has independently concluded that *heavily iced coffee* is the winning proposition for Iraq and has put capital behind it. That is third-party market validation of SHABM's core category thesis, delivered by someone with no incentive to flatter it. **Frame it that way.**
- **But it is also a clock.** Half Million and Kyan are both entering Iraq *now*, with Gulf balance sheets, established supply chains, and franchise systems. **SHABM's window to establish the ice category in Iraq before a well-capitalised Saudi chain does is short.** An investor will see this. Pre-empt them: this is a *speed* argument for the raise, and it is the honest one.
- **SHABM's defensible differentiation against them is exactly the part they cannot cheaply copy:** Half Million and Kyan sell iced coffee in a paper cup. SHABM sells iced coffee *in a carved ice vessel you eat*. The differentiation is the physical format and the capital behind it, not the coffee.

## 2.5 Salt (Kuwait) — proof the Gulf produces exportable Instagram-native brands

| Fact | Value | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | **Kuwait, ~2015**, began as a food truck / small burger concept | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| Identity | Stark black-and-white minimalist branding, hero burger + shakes; queues as brand signature | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| Regional spread | Kuwait → Saudi, UAE, Bahrain, Qatar, Egypt; international expansion reported incl. London | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] **low — verify** |
| Unit count | **[ESTIMATE] ~40–70 across GCC** — derived from typical Gulf multi-market chain density; **not sourced** | [ESTIMATE] low |

**The lesson:** Salt is the existence proof that **a Gulf-origin concept with a single hero product, a photogenic identity and no legacy heritage can scale across six-plus MENA markets by franchise within a decade.** SHABM's regional expansion plan (Saudi, UAE, Egypt, Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan) is not novel — it is a well-trodden path with living precedents. That materially de-risks the franchise slide. **The Salt route is the template; the pitch should name it.**

## 2.6 Kaak Al Manara (Lebanon) — heritage street food → franchised brand

**[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-low.** Lebanese *kaak* (sesame bread ring) — a centuries-old street food — was reformatted into a modern branded, franchised chain operating across Lebanon and into Saudi, UAE, Qatar and Kuwait.

**Why this is the most *culturally* relevant analog for SHABM:** it proves that **taking something ancient, local and unbranded, and wrapping it in modern retail design, is a validated MENA franchise strategy.** SHABM is doing exactly this: the name شبم is classical Arabic for the coldness of water, and Iraq has a documented living ice-block street economy (Baghdad ice plants run 24h at full capacity through summer, ice blocks retail at **IQD 4,000** — **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed / 964media).

**The deck line this unlocks:** *SHABM is not importing a foreign novelty into Iraq. It is taking something Baghdad already buys every single summer day — a block of ice — and making it the product instead of the packaging.* That framing is worth more than any market-size number, because it converts the concept from "trend" to "category."

## 2.7 Emack & Bolio's — a 50-year-old brand rescued by one visual gimmick, monetised in MENA

**[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med.** Boston ice cream brand, founded **1975**. Achieved a second life in the 2010s on the back of **cereal-coated cones** (Froot Loops, Rice Krispies) — a purely visual innovation with near-zero food cost — and converted that attention into **international franchising, with a notable Gulf presence (UAE, Kuwait, Saudi)**.

**Two lessons:**
1. **The visual gimmick is a marketing asset with a cost of goods measured in cents.** SHABM's frost-bloom, the ice block, and the fruit-shaped sorbets are the same trick with better physics.
2. **The Gulf is where visual ice-cream concepts get monetised.** MENA franchisees actively seek Instagram-native dessert formats. **SHABM's franchise pipeline is a real market, not a hypothesis.**

## 2.8 Somi Somi & Snowy Village — novelty-format frozen dessert with a decade of durability

**[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-low.** **Somi Somi** (Los Angeles, founded ~2016) sells the *ah-boong*: a fish-shaped taiyaki cone filled with custard or Nutella, topped with soft serve. It expanded to roughly **20–30 US locations** and has operated for ~a decade. **Snowy Village** (Korean-American, bingsu + taiyaki) franchised to a similar order of magnitude.

**Why this matters more than its size:** it is a **direct durability counter-example** to the "novelty shapes die" claim. A shaped, purely-photogenic frozen dessert format has now sustained ~10 years and a franchise network. **Cite this specifically when defending the fruit-shaped sorbet line.**

## 2.9 Sulbing / bingsu — the fastest café-format ramp on record, and its MENA presence

**[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-low.** **Sulbing (설빙)**, founded **2013 in Busan**, scaled to roughly **490 stores in Korea within about two years** — one of the most rapid café-format franchise ramps ever documented — then expanded internationally. Bingsu (shaved milk ice with toppings) also travelled through Caffe Bene's international network.

**MENA presence: [GAP].** Bingsu is *present* in Gulf Korean-dessert cafés (Dubai, Riyadh) but I cannot verify named operators, counts or pricing. **Research this properly — it is the closest existing competitor category to SHABM's frozen-dessert side in the Gulf, and its absence or thinness in Baghdad is a whitespace claim worth quantifying.**

**Relevance:** bingsu proves that **"ice as the dish, not the coolant" is a proven, franchisable, multi-hundred-unit café category** — just proven in Korea rather than the Arab world. SHABM is arguing that the same insight applies in the hottest capital in the region. That is a strong, honest analogy.

## 2.10 Suntory "-196" — a cryogenic *number* sustained as a brand for two decades

**[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med.** Suntory's **"-196"** is a Japanese canned chūhai launched around **2005**, named for its production process: whole fruit frozen at **−196°C** (liquid nitrogen) and pulverised before infusion. It became a major Japanese RTD brand and was launched into the **US market in 2024**, with mass-market advertising following.

**This is the most important durability datapoint in the entire document for SHABM's "-80" line.** It establishes that:
- **A temperature written as a number can function as a brand asset for ~20 years.** "-196" is not a trend, it is trade dress.
- The number works because it **encodes a real process claim**, not a gimmick. It answers "why does this taste different."

**Direct instruction for the deck: "-80" should be positioned as a *sub-brand and a process claim*, not a stunt.** "-80" is the name of a product line SHABM owns; the frost is the evidence. Trademark "-80" alongside شبم in classes 30, 32 and 43. (The sibling report already flags: file in both Latin and Arabic script, before launch, because Iraq is first-to-file in practice and pendency is 12–24 months — **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**.)

## 2.11 The cautionary cases — put these in the appendix and be seen to know them

| Case | Arc | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| **Dalgona coffee** | Korean whipped instant coffee. Global explosion **~March–April 2020** (COVID lockdowns); Google Trends collapsed by **~June 2020**. **~8–12 week half-life.** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high on arc |
| **Chicecream / 钟薛高** | Chinese premium ice cream, founded ~2018, viral growth on price and design; **"won't melt" scandal July 2022**; collapse, with the founder reportedly placed on a debt-enforcement list and livestream-selling to repay creditors by 2024. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med on arc, low on numbers |
| **Cereal Killer Cafe** (London) | Single-product novelty café, opened **Dec 2014** Brick Lane; **closed ~2020–21.** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| **Rainbow bagel** (The Bagel Store, Brooklyn) | Viral **2016**; store closed ~2019–20. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-low |
| **Liquid-nitrogen "Dragon's Breath"** | Viral ~2017–18; **US FDA issued a safety warning (Aug 2018)** about liquid nitrogen added to food/drink immediately before consumption, citing severe injury risk; UK hospitalisation reported. Category suppressed by regulators. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] **med — and directly relevant, see §3.1** |
| **10Below Ice Cream** (NYC) | Rolled ice cream, queues **2015–17**, subsequently contracted. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-low |

**The single most instructive contrast — put it on a slide:**

> **Dalgona coffee died in ten weeks. The cronut is still sold twelve years later.**
>
> Dalgona was a *recipe* — infinitely reproducible at home with instant coffee and a whisk. There was no operator, no capital, no scarcity, nothing to buy.
> The cronut (Dominique Ansel Bakery, launched **May 2013**) was a *product made in a bakery* — it required lamination, equipment, a named chef and a queue, and it sat inside a **full bakery menu with a daily habit business underneath it**.
>
> **SHABM is structurally a cronut, not a dalgona.** You cannot make a −80°C frozen cup, a hand-carved clear ice vessel or live rolled ice cream at home. That is the whole argument.

# 3. THE FIVE PRODUCT FORMATS — WHO IS ACTUALLY DOING THEM

## 3.1 The "-80" ultra-cold frozen-cup latte

**Finding, stated bluntly: [GAP]. I could not identify a single named commercial café, anywhere, running a −80°C frozen-cup latte as a menu item.** I searched my knowledge across the English, Chinese (`-80度 拿铁`, `零下80度冰咖啡`), Japanese (`冷凍カップ`) and Korean (`아이스라떼 -80`) formulations given in the brief and cannot name an operator.

**This is a two-sided finding and the deck must present both sides — presenting only the upside will get caught:**

- **Upside: this is genuine whitespace.** If it were an established format there would be named operators and price points. There aren't. **Frame it as "we could find no commercial operator of this format worldwide" — which is a much stronger and more honest claim than "it's a global trend."**
- **Downside: it is therefore unproven.** No operator has demonstrated that customers will pay a premium for it repeatedly. **Do not describe "-80" as a proven format. Describe it as the invention.** An investor will respect the distinction and punish the elision.

**The adjacent formats that *are* commercially proven — use these as the evidence base instead:**

| Proven adjacent format | Evidence | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| **Frozen/frosted glassware** | Near-universal bar convention; mugs held at ~−10 to −20°C. Zero novelty risk, decades of consumer acceptance. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |
| **Kirin "Frozen Beer"** (Ichiban Frozen Garden) | Japanese commercial product launched **~2012**: beer topped with foam frozen to ~−5°C, licensed into bars; major Japan/Asia rollout. **Proves consumers pay a premium for a visibly-frozen serve of an ordinary drink.** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| **Suntory "-196"** | §2.10 — a cryogenic temperature as a 20-year brand. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |
| **Liquid-nitrogen coffee/ice cream** | Commercially widespread 2015–18, then **regulator-suppressed after injury incidents (FDA warning Aug 2018)**. | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med |

### How the freeze actually works — and the safety issue nobody has flagged yet

**Equipment.** A −80°C serve requires a **laboratory ultra-low-temperature (ULT) freezer** — the same class of unit used for biological samples (Thermo Fisher, Eppendorf, Haier Biomedical, Panasonic/PHCbi). Chest or upright, typically 300–700 L.

- **[ESTIMATE] Capex: US$8,000–25,000 per unit** (new; 300–700 L). Derivation: standard lab-equipment price bands for ULT freezers. **Verify with a live quote — this is a major capex line and it belongs in the model, not in a footnote.**
- **[ESTIMATE] Energy: ~8–20 kWh/day steady-state**, with substantially higher draw during pull-down and after each door opening. Derivation: published ULT freezer efficiency bands (efficient models ~6–13 kWh/day; older/larger units higher). **A retail unit opening its ULT freezer dozens of times per hour during service will sit at or above the top of this range** — retail duty cycle is nothing like lab duty cycle.

**⚠️ This collides head-on with the sibling report's single biggest operating risk. [SESSION-VERIFIED]:** Baghdad's grid delivers **8–12 hours/day at best** (Middle East Monitor, Aug 2026); generator capacity costs **~US$8.40/ampere/month** (*Renewable Energies* journal, Jan 2025), with operator quotes reaching **IQD 25,000 (~$19)/ampere in summer**. **A ULT freezer cannot be power-cycled** — intermittent operation either destroys the compressor or loses the entire frozen-cup inventory, and its pull-down cycle is long and energy-expensive. **The −80 line requires genuinely uninterrupted power: dedicated on-site generation plus a UPS bridge, not neighbourhood ampere subscription.** Put this in capex. An investor with Iraq experience will ask, and "we hadn't costed that" is a fatal answer.

**⚠️ Product-safety issue — flag this to the founders now, before launch, not after.** A solid surface at **−80°C in contact with wet lips will cause cold burns and tissue adhesion within seconds.** This is the same physics as a tongue on frozen metal, at a far lower temperature. The Dragon's Breath / liquid-nitrogen precedent (§2.11) shows exactly how this ends: **one injury video travels further than a thousand frost videos, and regulators suppress the whole category.** Mitigations to design in from unit one:

1. **Material choice.** Use a **low-thermal-conductivity vessel — thick ceramic or borosilicate glass, never metal.** Metal at −80°C is dangerous; ceramic conducts heat away from the lip far more slowly.
2. **Mandatory temper window.** Serve on a wooden or cork base and build a **60–90 second "watch the frost bloom" ritual** into service. **The safety measure *is* the theatre** — the customer is filming during exactly the window in which the vessel becomes safe. This is the best single design idea in this report: it converts a liability into the content.
3. **Straw-first service** for the initial minute, plus a sleeve or handle so the vessel is never gripped bare-handed.
4. **Consider serving at −20 to −40°C for lip contact** and reserving true −80 for the reveal moment. The frost bloom — the actual visual — occurs at any temperature well below ambient dew point. **You do not need −80 for the shot; you need it for the name.**

## 3.2 Iced coffee served in a carved ice block / ice cup

**[GAP] on named operators and price points.** I cannot verify specific Japanese cafés (`氷のグラス` / ice-cup coffee) with names and prices. **This is the single most important gap to fill on re-run** — it is SHABM's flagship product and the deck needs at least two named precedents with prices.

**What I can establish with reasonable confidence — the supply chain, which is the part investors actually probe:**

- **Clear ice is a solved industrial problem.** It is produced by **directional freezing** — freezing water from one direction while circulating it, so dissolved gases and impurities are pushed out rather than trapped as the white cloudy core. This is standard craft-cocktail and ice-sculpture practice.
- **The standard machine class is the Clinebell block maker** (e.g. CB300 twin-block units, producing ~300 lb / ~136 kg blocks of optically clear ice). **[ESTIMATE] US$8,000–12,000 per machine**, derived from the US craft-bar equipment market. **Verify with a live quote.**
- **Craft cocktail bars worldwide already run in-house clear-ice programmes** — carving blocks into spheres, large-format cubes and vessels. **The skill, tooling (band saws, CNC ice carving, hot-plate levellers) and supply chain all exist commercially.** SHABM is not inventing ice carving; it is inventing a *retail café format built around it.*
- **[SESSION-VERIFIED] constraint:** the sibling cost report already models the ice-block vessel at **US$0.35 in-house clear-ice cost against a $6.50 price, ~87% gross margin** — the highest-margin item on SHABM's menu — while noting it is *"the most capital-intensive inventory per gram in the store,"* representing days of accumulated freezing energy per unit.
- **[SESSION-VERIFIED] food-safety constraint:** because the vessel is *eaten*, municipal water is not usable. **Minimum RO + UV multi-stage filtration with documented testing is mandatory**, and Baghdad's health-licence instructions explicitly name **"مثلجات" (iced products/frozen desserts)** as a supervised category.

**Strategic read:** the ice-block vessel is simultaneously SHABM's **highest-margin item, its strongest visual asset, its hardest capacity constraint, and its largest food-safety exposure.** It should be positioned as the **halo product with a daily cap**, not the volume driver. Cap it, publicise the cap, and let it sell the rest of the menu. (This is exactly the FIX Dessert Chocolatier playbook from §2.1.)

## 3.3 Thai rolled ice cream — saturated in the West, plausible second life in MENA

**[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med on the arc, low on MENA specifics.**

- **Origin:** Thai street food (*I-Tim-Pad*), pan-fried/scraped ice cream rolls.
- **Viral cycle:** exploded in the US ~**2015–2016** via short-form food video; Google Trends peaked ~**2016–17**; deflated from ~2018.
- **Peak operators:** **10Below Ice Cream** (NYC, 2015, queues around the block, later contracted); **Sweet Charlie's** (Philadelphia, ~2016, franchised aggressively, reported international franchising including into the Middle East — **verify**).
- **Current state in the West: saturated and commoditised.** Standalone rolled-ice-cream shops largely failed; the format survives as a *station inside broader dessert cafés.*

**The correct conclusion for SHABM, and it is a favourable one:**

> **Do not build a brand on rolled ice cream. Build a station.**

Rolled ice cream's failure mode in the US was **single-product standalone stores**, not the product itself. As one of five lines inside a broader cold-concept café — where coffee carries the habit business — it contributes:
- **live theatre at the counter** (the strongest in-store content generator on the menu, and it runs continuously),
- **a low price point (US$4.50 at ~78% gross margin — [SESSION-VERIFIED])** that captures the student segment the sibling report identifies as *"strong for volume, weak for ticket"* at Al-Jadriya,
- **infinite flavour rotation** — the Crumbl mechanic (§2.2) at near-zero cost.

**On MENA saturation: [GAP].** Rolled ice cream is present in Gulf dessert cafés but I cannot quantify penetration in Baghdad. **This matters — if Baghdad already has rolled ice cream on ten corners, it is a commodity station, not a differentiator. Check it with physical fieldwork, not desk research.**

## 3.4 Fruit-shaped frozen sorbets

**Brand-level finding: [GAP] and one correction.**

- **Correction to the brief:** *frutta martorana* is **Sicilian marzipan** (almond paste sculpted and painted as fruit) — it is **not frozen**. The frozen tradition you want is **Sicilian *frutta gelata* / sorbetto served in the hollowed-out real fruit shell** (lemon, orange, coconut) — a long-established Italian format sold both in gelaterie and as a frozen retail SKU in European supermarkets. **[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med.** Getting this distinction wrong in front of an Italian-speaking investor would be costly; getting it right is a credibility marker.
- **Rellatto, ICY FRU, The Bakery "Fruity Vibes": [GAP] — I could not verify any of these three brands, their products, box prices or production methods.** **Do not cite them until verified.**

**What I *can* give you, and it is the operationally useful part — how these are actually produced at scale:**

The modern fruit-*shaped* (moulded, not shelled) sorbet is a **standard patisserie entremet technique**, industrialised:

1. **Silicone moulds.** The category-defining suppliers are **Silikomart** (Italy — the *3Design* series includes hyper-realistic fruit forms) and **Pavoni / Pavoflex** (Italy). **[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-high.** These are off-the-shelf, cheap, and food-safe. The sibling report already prices **plastic ice-block moulds at IQD 1,000/piece** locally — **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**, though silicone entremet moulds are imported and cost far more.
2. **Two-part construction.** Outer shell = fruit-purée sorbet, frozen against the mould wall; inner core = a contrasting insert (coulis, a second sorbet, a liquid centre) frozen separately in a smaller mould and inserted. This is what produces the "cut it open" reveal — **the second content moment, after the shape itself.**
3. **Blast freezing.** A blast freezer (−35 to −40°C) sets the mould in minutes rather than hours. Non-negotiable for throughput and for ice-crystal texture.
4. **Velvet/flocked finish.** The realistic matte fruit skin is produced with a **spray gun applying warmed cocoa butter + colour onto the frozen surface**, which sets instantly into a velvet texture. This is the single technique that makes them look like real fruit rather than like moulded dessert.
5. **Stem/leaf garnish** — chocolate or sugar-paste, applied at plating.

**Why this line may be SHABM's most durable, and the argument to make:**
- **[SESSION-VERIFIED] economics: US$0.75 COGS against a $4.00 price — ~81% gross margin, in-season.**
- **It is the only line that is not a live performance** — therefore the only line that is **shelf-stable in-freezer, pre-producible off-peak, giftable, boxable, and sellable as multi-unit takeaway.** Everything else on SHABM's menu must be consumed within metres and minutes.
- **It is the only line that survives delivery.** The sibling report is emphatic that the −80 cup, the ice block and live rolled ice cream **cannot survive a delivery journey in 45°C Baghdad** — **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**. **A boxed set of six fruit-shaped sorbets in an insulated box can.**
- **It is the natural franchise and retail-channel product** — the SKU that eventually goes into Gulf supermarkets and hotel minibars.

> **Deck recommendation: reposition the fruit sorbets from "product line 4" to "the second business."** They are the answer to "what happens when the spectacle fades," to "how do you use delivery," and to "how does this become more than a chain of kiosks." **Right now the concept treats them as a menu item. They are the hedge.**

# 4. DURABILITY — THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES THE ROUND

**Assume the first substantive question from any competent investor is: *"This is a trend. What happens in year three?"* The deck must have a slide that answers it before it is asked.**

## 4.1 Base rates — the honest numbers

**The 90% failure myth is false, and knowing that is itself a credibility marker.** The definitive academic work is **H.G. Parsa et al., "Why Restaurants Fail," *Cornell Hotel and Restaurant Administration Quarterly*, 2005** (with a follow-up circa 2011). **[MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-high.**

| Metric | Value | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Year-1 restaurant failure | **~26–27%** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-high (Parsa 2005) |
| Cumulative 3-year failure | **~59–60%** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med-high (Parsa 2005) |
| The "90% fail in year one" claim | **A myth. Not supported by the data.** | [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] high |

**Use it like this:** *"About 60% of restaurants fail within three years. The 90% figure is a myth. Here is specifically why concepts in our category fail, and here is what we have built to avoid each failure mode."* That is a far stronger posture than asserting the risk away.

## 4.2 The viral lifecycle — two completely different curves

**The most important analytical distinction in this document. [MODEL-KNOWLEDGE] med, derived from the pattern across §2.11 and §2.1–2.3.**

| Curve | What it is | Half-life | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Curve A — Recipe trend** | Reproducible at home. No operator, no capital, nothing to buy. | **4–12 weeks** | Dalgona coffee, cloud bread, feta pasta, butter boards |
| **Curve B — Retail format** | Requires equipment, premises, skill. Must be bought. | **12–24 months of peak attention, then either franchise-out or decay** | Rolled ice cream, cronut, Dubai chocolate, bingsu, Crumbl |

**SHABM is unambiguously Curve B — with the strongest Curve B characteristics of any example here**, because its barriers are *capital and cold chain*, the two hardest to replicate in Iraq specifically (where uninterrupted power is scarce and expensive — **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**). **The single greatest thing Baghdad's electricity crisis does for SHABM is act as a moat.** A competitor cannot casually add a −80 freezer and a clear-ice programme; they need generation capacity, capital and process knowledge. **Say this out loud in the deck — it turns the biggest operating risk into the competitive answer.**

**The corollary is a deadline.** Curve B gives ~12–24 months of peak attention. **The raise must be sized and sequenced to convert attention into units inside that window** — that is the honest justification for the amount being raised and for the franchise timeline.

## 4.3 What the survivors did — seven mechanisms

Extracted across every case above. **This should be an actual slide: "Seven things that separate survivors from casualties," with SHABM's answer next to each.**

| # | Mechanism | Who proves it | SHABM's answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **A habit product under the spectacle** | Cane's, Crumbl, cronut/Dominique Ansel | **Coffee, juice and cold drinks.** Spectacle acquires; caffeine and 45°C heat retain. |
| 2 | **Engineered rotation — a reason to return weekly** | Crumbl's 6-cookies-a-week | **Weekly flavour drop + seasonal Iraqi fruit calendar.** Free, because fruit is seasonal anyway. |
| 3 | **Daypart expansion** | All surviving cafés | **Hot barista drinks in winter is already in the concept — protect it.** Baghdad has a real winter; a pure ice concept is a ~6-month business. This line is not a footnote, it is survival. |
| 4 | **Menu breadth beyond the hero** | Cronut inside a full bakery; Cereal Killer Cafe died without it | **Five lines already. This is the concept's greatest structural strength — lead with it.** |
| 5 | **Franchise while attention is high** | Crumbl, Salt, Emack & Bolio's, Sulbing | **The purpose of this raise. Franchise-ready ops manual from unit one.** |
| 6 | **Own the format legally before you prove it** | FIX lost the category to Lindt and the grocers | **File شبم + "-80" in Arabic and Latin, classes 30/32/43, in Iraq and every target market, immediately. 12–24 month pendency; Iraq is not in Madrid. [SESSION-VERIFIED]** |
| 7 | **Never let a safety incident define the category** | Dragon's Breath / liquid nitrogen (FDA 2018) | **The temper ritual (§3.1), ceramic not metal, RO+UV water, documented HACCP from unit one. [SESSION-VERIFIED]** |

## 4.4 The durability architecture — how to actually structure the answer

**Do not argue that SHABM is not a trend. Argue that it is a trend *bolted onto* a non-trend, and show the split.**

Separate the P&L into two engines on the slide:

- **Engine 1 — The Spectacle (the −80 cup, the ice-block vessel, live rolled ice cream).** High margin (78–87% — **[SESSION-VERIFIED]**), high content output, **assume attention decays.** This engine's job is **customer acquisition at negative marketing cost** — the customers produce the advertising.
- **Engine 2 — The Habit (coffee, juice, slush, winter hot drinks, boxed fruit sorbets).** Repeat-purchase, weather-driven, delivery-compatible, all-season. **This engine's job is to still be there in year five.**

**Then state the test explicitly, and take the hit:**

> *"Model the spectacle at zero in year three. If the unit still clears its rent on coffee, juice and boxed sorbets alone, the business is not a trend — the trend is just the cheapest customer-acquisition channel we will ever have."*

**Ask the financial modelling agent to run precisely that scenario and put it in the deck as a downside case.** An investor who sees a founder voluntarily zero out their own hero product and still show a viable unit will stop asking whether it is a fad. **This is the single highest-leverage thing the deck can do**, and it costs nothing but honesty.

## 5.2 What a food Reel/TikTok must hit to move footfall — [ESTIMATE], low confidence

**No sourced MENA-specific F&B threshold is available to me. The following is a derivation, and it must be labelled as such on any slide.**

**Derivation method:** local-business social conversion generally runs at fractions of a percent of *local* reach; the binding variable is **geographic relevance**, not raw views. A million views in Cairo does nothing for a Baghdad kiosk.

| Tier | Local (Baghdad-geo) views | Expected effect | Tag |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noise | <50,000 | No measurable footfall | [ESTIMATE] |
| Detectable | 100,000–300,000 | Measurable same-week uplift | [ESTIMATE] |
| **Queue-forming** | **500,000+ local, or a creator >500K followers posting a located visit** | **Visible queue effect** | [ESTIMATE] |
| Category event | 2M+ / national press pickup | Competitor copying begins within weeks | [ESTIMATE] |

**The more reliable operating guidance, which does not depend on these numbers:**
1. **Saves and shares beat views.** A save is intent-to-visit. Track saves/1,000 views as the primary KPI, not view count.
2. **Location tags and Arabic-language captions decide whether reach is local.** Non-negotiable.
3. **The content must be produced by customers, not by the brand.** SHABM's entire physical design — a kiosk that looks like a melting ice cube, a vessel that frosts on camera, ice cream rolled in front of the customer — is a **camera-facing manufacturing decision.** Budget for **lighting the counter for vertical video** as a capex line. It is the cheapest marketing in the plan, and almost every operator forgets it.
4. **Design the failure of the shot.** Ensure the frost bloom (§3.1) is visible against the counter's backdrop colour. A dark matte backdrop behind a frosting white vessel is the difference between a viral shot and an unusable one.

# 8. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE DECK

1. **The concept sits on the right side of the durability line.** It is Curve B (capital-gated retail format), not Curve A (home-reproducible recipe). Dalgona died in ten weeks because anyone could make it. Nobody carves an ice vessel at home.
2. **The strongest single argument is menu breadth, and it is already in the concept.** Five lines, two engines, a winter daypart. Cereal Killer Cafe died of narrowness; the cronut survived twelve years inside a full bakery.
3. **Baghdad's power crisis is the moat.** State it explicitly. The thing that makes SHABM hard to operate is the same thing that makes it hard to copy.
4. **The fruit-shaped sorbets are being under-sold as "line 4."** They are the delivery-compatible, boxable, giftable, retail-channel, all-season hedge — the answer to three separate investor objections at once.
5. **Two clocks are running.** Kyan Café and Half Million are entering Iraq now with Gulf capital and the same "heavily iced" thesis; and Iraqi trademark pendency is 12–24 months in a first-to-file jurisdiction that is not in the Madrid Protocol. **File before launch, and let the speed argument justify the raise.**
6. **Volunteer the downside case.** Model the spectacle at zero in year three and show the unit still clearing rent on coffee, juice and boxed sorbets. **A founder who zeroes out their own hero product and still shows a viable unit stops being asked whether it's a fad.**
